title: Level 4 (Expert) - A-33
notes:
West's club opening lead is won in dummy. The contract will be easy if trumps are 3-2. If trumps are 4-1, South has two chances. He could either play to score his small trumps by ruffing dummy's clubs or play for a minor suit squeeze.

In either case, leading a club at trick 2 for a ruff in the closed hand is a good idea. If South is going to adopt the "squeeze line", ruffing a club will help to isolate the threat in that suit. If South is going to try to score all of his trumps, he must use each of dummy's 3 entries for club ruffs.

South should next cash the top trumps revealing that West began with a certain trump trick. South is now at the crossroads. If he chooses to play for a squeeze, he should surrender a trump trick at once. If East began with 4 or more diamonds along with 5 or more clubs, he can later be simple squeezed (or trump squeezed) on the run of the spades.

South gives himself slightly better odds, however, by playing to ruff all of dummy's clubs. West must have either 3415 or 3424 distribution for this line to succeed. South should begin by cashing 3 rounds of spades ending in the dummy. A second club is ruffed.

South cashes the ♦A and continues a low diamond. If West began with a singleton diamond, it will not help him to ruff (notice that if all of the spades had not been cashed earlier, West could defeat the contract by pitching a spade on the second diamond).

After dummy wins the ♦K, South leads dummy's last club and ruffs in the closed hand. West is forced to ruff his partner's diamond winner at trick 13.

The mathematics required to choose between the 2 lines of play are too complex for almost anyone to solve at the table. The odds of success of the 2 lines are very close but the "ruffing line" does give slightly better odds than the "squeeze line".
